HOME EQUITY SALES CONTRACT ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — A DIFFERENT TRANSACTION FROM A FORECLOSURE PROCESS
This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's Home Equity Sales Contract Act, Civil Code §§ 1695-1695.17. That statute is a completely different subject from the corpus's existing Notice of Default / Nonjudicial Foreclosure Process information sheet and its companion Homeowner Bill of Rights information sheet. Those two documents describe the process by which a lender or its trustee forecloses on a borrower under a deed of trust that already exists between the borrower and the lender. This sheet instead describes a separate, private transaction: the direct sale of a home by a distressed owner to an investor — called an "equity purchaser" under the statute — who is not the borrower's lender and is not conducting a foreclosure sale at all. It concerns a potential sale of the real property commonly known as 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield between Pat Morgan as equity seller and Jordan Lee as equity purchaser. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself create, cancel, rescind, or otherwise affect any contract for the sale of this or any other property; it does not determine whether 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield meets the statutory definition of "residence in foreclosure" or whether Jordan Lee meets the statutory definition of "equity purchaser"; and it does not determine whether any actual contract, notice, or practice relating to a sale of this property has complied — or failed to comply — with the requirements this sheet describes.

WHO THE ACT COVERS — "EQUITY PURCHASER," "RESIDENCE IN FORECLOSURE," AND "EQUITY SELLER"
The Home Equity Sales Contract Act applies only to transactions that fit its defined terms. Civil Code § 1695.1(a) provides that “Equity purchaser” means any person who acquires title to any residence in foreclosure, except a person who acquires such title as follows, and then lists exclusions including a purchase for use as a personal residence, a deed in lieu of foreclosure, a trustee's deed at a foreclosure sale, a statutorily authorized sale, a court order or judgment, or a transfer from a spouse or blood relative. Section 1695.1(b) defines “residence in foreclosure” (and “residential real property in foreclosure”) narrowly: it means "residential real property consisting of one- to four-family dwelling units, one of which the owner occupies as his or her principal place of residence, and against which there is an outstanding notice of default, recorded pursuant to Article 1 (commencing with Section 2920) of Chapter 2 of Title 14 of Part 4 of Division 3." A property does not meet this statutory definition merely because the owner is behind on payments or expects a foreclosure — a notice of default must actually have been recorded against it. Section 1695.1(c) provides that “Equity seller” means any seller of a residence in foreclosure, and section 1695.1(e) provides that “Contract” means any offer or any contract, agreement, or arrangement, or any term thereof, between an equity purchaser and equity seller incident to the sale of a residence in foreclosure. If a Notice of Default affecting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: August 1, 2026.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Equity purchaser” means any person who acquires title to any residence in foreclosure, except a person who acquires such title as follows:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.1(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.1.&lawCode=CIV)
  "“Residence in foreclosure” and “residential real property in foreclosure” means residential real property consisting of one- to four-family dwelling units, one of which the owner occupies as his or her principal place of residence, and against which there is an outstanding notice of default, recorded pursuant to Article 1 (commencing with Section 2920) of Chapter 2 of Title 14 of Part 4 of Division 3."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.1(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.1(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.1.&lawCode=CIV)
  "“Equity seller” means any seller of a residence in foreclosure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.1(c), (e) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.1(c), (e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.1.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This clause states the Act's own defined terms; it does not determine whether any particular property or transaction actually satisfies them — for example, whether a notice of default has in fact been recorded, whether the property is a one- to four-family dwelling occupied by its owner, or whether an exclusion (such as a purchase for use as a personal residence, or a purchase from a blood relative) applies to a particular buyer. Those are factual and legal determinations outside the scope of this information sheet. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass: a CourtListener case-law search returned a daily-quota error (HTTP 429, 125/day limit) before any case law could be checked, so this clause is not verified against how courts have applied these defined terms in practice.

REQUIRED CONTRACT FORM AND CONTENTS
The Act requires that a contract between an equity purchaser and an equity seller take a particular written form. Civil Code § 1695.2 requires that "Every contract shall be written in letters of a size equal to 10-point bold type, in the same language principally used by the equity purchaser and equity seller to negotiate the sale of the residence in foreclosure and shall be fully completed and signed and dated by the equity seller and equity purchaser prior to the execution of any instrument of conveyance of the residence in foreclosure." Section 1695.3 requires that "Every contract shall contain the entire agreement of the parties and shall include the following terms," including "The name, business address, and the telephone number of the equity purchaser," "The address of the residence in foreclosure," and "The total consideration to be given by the equity purchaser in connection with or incident to the sale," along with a description of payment terms, the time possession transfers, the terms of any rental agreement, a notice of cancellation, and a boldface warning statement naming the equity purchaser. A contract affecting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee that omits these statutorily required terms, or that is not in the required type size and language, does not comply with section 1695.2 or 1695.3 as written.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Every contract shall be written in letters of a size equal to 10-point bold type, in the same language principally used by the equity purchaser and equity seller to negotiate the sale of the residence in foreclosure and shall be fully completed and signed and dated by the equity seller and equity purchaser prior to the execution of any instrument of conveyance of the residence in foreclosure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.2 (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.2.&lawCode=CIV)
  "Every contract shall contain the entire agreement of the parties and shall include the following terms: (a) The name, business address, and the telephone number of the equity purchaser. (b) The address of the residence in foreclosure. (c) The total consideration to be given by the equity purchaser in connection with or incident to the sale."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.3 (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.3 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.3.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the statute's form and content requirements; it does not evaluate whether any specific contract for a particular sale in fact satisfies them (for example, its actual type size, its completeness, or the specific consideration and payment terms it states), and it does not reproduce every one of section 1695.3's eight lettered required-term subdivisions verbatim. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law on what counts as adequate compliance was reviewed.

THE SELLER'S STATUTORY RIGHT TO CANCEL
Civil Code § 1695.4(a) gives every equity seller a statutory cancellation right independent of any other rescission right: "In addition to any other right of rescission, the equity seller has the right to cancel any contract with an equity purchaser until midnight of the fifth business day following the day on which the equity seller signs a contract that complies with this chapter or until 8 a.m. on the day scheduled for the sale of the property pursuant to a power of sale conferred in a deed of trust, whichever occurs first." "Business day" excludes Sundays and the enumerated statutory holidays under section 1695.1(d). Section 1695.4(b) states that "Cancellation occurs when the equity seller personally delivers written notice of cancellation to the address specified in the contract or sends a telegram indicating cancellation to that address." Section 1695.4(c) adds that "A notice of cancellation given by the equity seller need not take the particular form as provided with the contract and, however expressed, is effective if it indicates the intention of the equity seller not to be bound by the contract." A contract affecting 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield signed by Pat Morgan on September 1, 2026 would, under this section, remain cancellable through the statutory period described above, unless a scheduled trustee's sale cuts that period short.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In addition to any other right of rescission, the equity seller has the right to cancel any contract with an equity purchaser until midnight of the fifth business day following the day on which the equity seller signs a contract that complies with this chapter or until 8 a.m. on the day scheduled for the sale of the property pursuant to a power of sale conferred in a deed of trust, whichever occurs first."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.4(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.4(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.4.&lawCode=CIV)
  "A notice of cancellation given by the equity seller need not take the particular form as provided with the contract and, however expressed, is effective if it indicates the intention of the equity seller not to be bound by the contract."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.4(b), (c) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.4(b), (c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.4.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This clause states the general statutory cancellation period and its two possible end points; it does not calculate the specific date and time by which cancellation must occur for any actual contract, which depends on the signing date, the applicable business days and holidays, and whether a foreclosure sale has been scheduled and for what date. It also does not address the separate cancellation-form requirements of section 1695.5, covered in a companion clause. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

REQUIRED CANCELLATION NOTICE AND WARNING LANGUAGE
The Act requires that the seller's cancellation right be disclosed in specific, prominent language attached to the contract. Civil Code § 1695.5(a) requires the contract to contain, near the seller's signature line, a statutory notice — in at least 12-point bold type — telling the seller that the sale may be cancelled without any penalty or obligation before a stated date and time, and directing the seller to an attached notice-of-cancellation form. Section 1695.5(b) requires that "The contract shall be accompanied by a completed form in duplicate, captioned “notice of cancellation” in a size equal to 12-point bold type, if the contract is printed or in capital letters if the contract is typed," containing statutory language allowing the seller to cancel by personally delivering a signed and dated copy of the notice, or sending a telegram, to the purchaser's stated business address before the stated deadline. Section 1695.5(c) requires that "The equity purchaser shall provide the equity seller with a copy of the contract and the attached notice of cancellation." Section 1695.5(d) provides that "Until the equity purchaser has complied with this section, the equity seller may cancel the contract" — meaning the seller's cancellation window does not close if the purchaser never gives the required notice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The equity purchaser shall provide the equity seller with a copy of the contract and the attached notice of cancellation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.5(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.5.&lawCode=CIV)
  "The contract shall be accompanied by a completed form in duplicate, captioned “notice of cancellation” in a size equal to 12-point bold type, if the contract is printed or in capital letters if the contract is typed"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.5(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.5.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This clause paraphrases, rather than quotes, the exact wording of the statutory cancellation warning in section 1695.5(a) itself, because the copy of that subdivision obtained from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov contains what appears to be a stray line-break formatting artifact inside the word "without" in the official site's HTML; the surrounding subdivisions quoted directly below were unaffected. This clause also does not certify that any actual notice-of-cancellation form used for a particular sale matches the required type size, language, and content. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

PRACTICES PROHIBITED DURING THE CANCELLATION PERIOD AND GENERALLY
The Act restricts what an equity purchaser may do while a seller's cancellation right is still open, and prohibits certain misrepresentations at any time. Civil Code § 1695.6(b) provides: "Until the time within which the equity seller may cancel the transaction has fully elapsed, the equity purchaser shall not do any of the following," and then lists accepting or inducing execution of any instrument of conveyance, recording any document signed by the seller, transferring or encumbering any interest in the property, and paying the seller any consideration. Section 1695.6(c) requires that "Within 10 days following receipt of a notice of cancellation given in accordance with Sections 1695.4 and 1695.5, the equity purchaser shall return without condition any original contract and any other documents signed by the equity seller." Section 1695.6(d) separately prohibits an equity purchaser, without a time limit, from making "untrue or misleading statements regarding the value of the residence in foreclosure, the amount of proceeds the equity seller will receive after a foreclosure sale, any contract term, the equity seller's rights or obligations incident to or arising out of the sale transaction, the nature of any document which the equity purchaser induces the equity seller to sign, or any other untrue or misleading statement concerning the sale of the residence in foreclosure to the equity purchaser." Separately, section 1695.13 makes it "unlawful for any person to initiate, enter into, negotiate, or consummate any transaction involving residential real property in foreclosure, as defined in Section 1695.1, if such person, by the terms of such transaction, takes unconscionable advantage of the property owner in foreclosure."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Until the time within which the equity seller may cancel the transaction has fully elapsed, the equity purchaser shall not do any of the following:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.6(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.6(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.6.&lawCode=CIV)
  "Within 10 days following receipt of a notice of cancellation given in accordance with Sections 1695.4 and 1695.5, the equity purchaser shall return without condition any original contract and any other documents signed by the equity seller."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.6(c) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.6(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.6.&lawCode=CIV)
  "It is unlawful for any person to initiate, enter into, negotiate, or consummate any transaction involving residential real property in foreclosure, as defined in Section 1695.1, if such person, by the terms of such transaction, takes unconscionable advantage of the property owner in foreclosure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.13 (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.13 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.13.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This clause states the categories of conduct the statute prohibits; it does not evaluate whether any specific conduct by a particular equity purchaser toward a particular equity seller falls within them, and "unconscionable advantage" under section 1695.13 is an undefined statutory standard this sheet does not attempt to apply. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law interpreting "unconscionable advantage" or the section 1695.6 prohibitions was reviewed.

CIVIL REMEDIES, RESCISSION OF COMPLETED SALES, AND CRIMINAL PENALTIES
The Act backs its requirements with layered remedies. Civil Code § 1695.7 gives an equity seller a civil action for a violation of section 1695.6 or 1695.13: "An equity seller may bring an action for the recovery of damages or other equitable relief against an equity purchaser for a violation of any subdivision of Section 1695.6 or Section 1695.13. The equity seller shall recover actual damages plus reasonable attorneys' fees and costs." The court may additionally award exemplary damages or equitable relief, and for a violation of the section 1695.6(b)(3) transfer-or-encumbrance prohibition or of section 1695.13, the court "shall award exemplary damages in an amount not less than three times the equity seller's actual damages" or, alternatively, "a civil penalty of up to two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500)" — but not both — with any such action to be "commenced within four years after the date of the alleged violation." Separately, even after a sale has closed, section 1695.14(a) makes a transaction that violates section 1695.13 voidable, and "the transaction may be rescinded by the property owner within two years of the date of the recordation of the conveyance of the residential real property in foreclosure," subject to the protections for a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer for value described in section 1695.14(c). Beyond civil liability, section 1695.8 makes a violation of section 1695.6, or conduct "which would operate as a fraud or deceit upon an equity seller," punishable "upon conviction" by "a fine of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), by imprisonment in the county jail for not more than one year," or both.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An equity seller may bring an action for the recovery of damages or other equitable relief against an equity purchaser for a violation of any subdivision of Section 1695.6 or Section 1695.13. The equity seller shall recover actual damages plus reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.7 (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.7 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.7.&lawCode=CIV)
  "In any transaction involving residential real property in foreclosure, as defined in Section 1695.1, which is in violation of Section 1695.13 is voidable and the transaction may be rescinded by the property owner within two years of the date of the recordation of the conveyance of the residential real property in foreclosure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.14(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.14(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.14.&lawCode=CIV)
  "Any equity purchaser who violates any subdivision of Section 1695.6 or who engages in any practice which would operate as a fraud or deceit upon an equity seller shall, upon conviction, be punished by a fine of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), by imprisonment in the county jail for not more than one year"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1695.8 (California Legislative Information text), Civ. C. § 1695.8 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1695.8.&lawCode=CIV)
  Known gap: This clause states the remedies and penalties the statute makes available; it does not determine whether any violation has occurred with respect to a particular property or transaction, does not calculate any specific damages, penalty, or limitations deadline, and does not address how these civil remedies interact with the separate criminal penalty in section 1695.8 (for example, whether both can apply to the same conduct). Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law applying these remedy provisions was reviewed.

expectedJSON.body: The Act restricts what an equity purchaser may do while a seller's cancellation right is still open, and prohibits certain misrepresentations at any time. Civil Code § 1695.6(b) provides: "Until the time within which the equity seller may cancel the transaction has fully elapsed, the equity purchaser shall not do any of the following," and then lists accepting or inducing execution of any instrument of conveyance, recording any document signed by the seller, transferring or encumbering any interest in the property, and paying the seller any consideration. Section 1695.6(c) requires that "Within 10 days following receipt of a notice of cancellation given in accordance with Sections 1695.4 and 1695.5, the equity purchaser shall return without condition any original contract and any other documents signed by the equity seller." Section 1695.6(d) separately prohibits an equity purchaser, without a time limit, from making "untrue or misleading statements regarding the value of the residence in foreclosure, the amount of proceeds the equity seller will receive after a foreclosure sale, any contract term, the equity seller's rights or obligations incident to or arising out of the sale transaction, the nature of any document which the equity purchaser induces the equity seller to sign, or any other untrue or misleading statement concerning the sale of the residence in foreclosure to the equity purchaser." Separately, section 1695.13 makes it "unlawful for any person to initiate, enter into, negotiate, or consummate any transaction involving residential real property in foreclosure, as defined in Section 1695.1, if such person, by the terms of such transaction, takes unconscionable advantage of the property owner in foreclosure."

expectedJSON.body: The Act backs its requirements with layered remedies. Civil Code § 1695.7 gives an equity seller a civil action for a violation of section 1695.6 or 1695.13: "An equity seller may bring an action for the recovery of damages or other equitable relief against an equity purchaser for a violation of any subdivision of Section 1695.6 or Section 1695.13. The equity seller shall recover actual damages plus reasonable attorneys' fees and costs." The court may additionally award exemplary damages or equitable relief, and for a violation of the section 1695.6(b)(3) transfer-or-encumbrance prohibition or of section 1695.13, the court "shall award exemplary damages in an amount not less than three times the equity seller's actual damages" or, alternatively, "a civil penalty of up to two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500)" — but not both — with any such action to be "commenced within four years after the date of the alleged violation." Separately, even after a sale has closed, section 1695.14(a) makes a transaction that violates section 1695.13 voidable, and "the transaction may be rescinded by the property owner within two years of the date of the recordation of the conveyance of the residential real property in foreclosure," subject to the protections for a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer for value described in section 1695.14(c). Beyond civil liability, section 1695.8 makes a violation of section 1695.6, or conduct "which would operate as a fraud or deceit upon an equity seller," punishable "upon conviction" by "a fine of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), by imprisonment in the county jail for not more than one year," or both.
